title: Sumatriptan and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Imitrex, Maxalt, and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on sumatriptan (Imitrex)? How triptans and alcohol interact, how long to wait, why a hangover isn't a migraine, rizatriptan notes, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on sumatriptan (Imitrex)? How triptans and alcohol interact, how long to wait, rizatriptan (Maxalt) notes, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** sumatriptan (brand name Imitrex) does not have a known dangerous chemical interaction with alcohol. Your body breaks the two down in different ways, and the drug's prescribing information does not list alcohol as a reason not to take it. The real problems are practical ones. Alcohol is one of the most common migraine triggers, so drinking can bring on the very attack you're treating. Both sumatriptan and alcohol can make you dizzy and drowsy, and those effects add up. And a hangover headache is not a migraine, so reaching for a triptan the morning after a big night usually isn't the right move. This guide explains how the two interact, how long to wait, what's different about rizatriptan (Maxalt) and the other triptans, and the warning signs that need a doctor.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink during a migraine attack or right after taking a dose. Give the attack time to fully clear and the drug a few hours to wear off before having a drink. Don't use sumatriptan for an ordinary hangover headache unless your doctor has told you to. If you also take an antidepressant, a combination pill with naproxen, or anything else that affects serotonin or your stomach, ask your pharmacist how alcohol fits in. And never take sumatriptan if you have chest pain, heart disease, or uncontrolled high blood pressure unless your doctor has cleared it.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your medicine and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before combining sumatriptan with alcohol if** you have heart disease or risk factors for it, high blood pressure, liver problems, or a history of stroke, if you take an antidepressant or other serotonin-affecting drug, or if you're using triptans more than a few days a month. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you have chest pain or pressure that doesn't fade quickly, pain spreading to your arm, jaw, or back, sudden weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, a sudden "worst headache of your life," or agitation, fever, fast heartbeat, and muscle twitching after taking sumatriptan.

## How Sumatriptan Works, in Plain Words

Sumatriptan belongs to a group of migraine drugs called **triptans**. It's a prescription medicine in most countries, sold as tablets (usually 25, 50, or 100 mg), a nasal spray, and an injection. Generic sumatriptan is widely available, and brand names include Imitrex in the US and Imigran in the UK and elsewhere.

During a migraine, blood vessels around the brain widen and nerves in the area release inflammatory chemicals that drive the pain. Sumatriptan mimics serotonin at two specific receptor types (called 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D). Switching those receptors on does two things: it narrows the widened blood vessels and it calms the release of those pain chemicals. That's why it works on migraine specifically and doesn't do much for most other kinds of headache.

A few details that matter when alcohol enters the picture:

- **It's short-acting.** Sumatriptan's half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half the dose) is about two hours. Most of the drug is gone within roughly ten hours.
- **It's broken down by an enzyme called MAO-A**, not by the liver enzymes that handle alcohol. That's the main reason there's no well-documented chemical clash between the two.
- **It narrows blood vessels.** This is the reason it isn't safe for people with heart disease, and the reason chest tightness is a known side effect.
- **It works best early.** Triptans are most effective when taken at the start of the headache phase, not hours into it.

## Is It Safe to Mix Sumatriptan and Alcohol?

There's no evidence of a direct, dangerous interaction between sumatriptan and alcohol at normal doses. The US prescribing information for Imitrex does not list alcohol as a contraindication, and the drug doesn't share a metabolic pathway with alcohol the way acetaminophen does. If you had a glass of wine with dinner and a migraine starts later that evening, taking your prescribed dose is not known to be dangerous in itself.

That's not the same as saying the combination is a good idea. Here's where the real risks sit.

### 1. Side effects stack

Sumatriptan commonly causes dizziness, drowsiness, a heavy or tired feeling, tingling, and warm or flushed skin. Alcohol causes dizziness and drowsiness too. Put them together and you can feel more impaired than you'd expect from either one alone. That matters if you plan to drive, look after kids, or walk home. The label already warns that sumatriptan can make you drowsy or dizzy and to be careful with driving until you know how it affects you. Alcohol makes that warning more important, not less.

### 2. Alcohol can trigger or worsen the migraine

This is the biggest practical problem. Alcohol is one of the triggers people with migraine report most often, and red wine has the strongest reputation. Drinking during or soon after an attack can make it last longer, bring it back after the triptan wears off (a "rebound" or recurrent attack), or set off a new one. Alcohol also dehydrates you and disrupts sleep, and poor sleep and dehydration are classic migraine triggers in their own right. For more on why this happens, see our guide to [migraine after drinking](/never-hungover/migraine-after-drinking).

### 3. Symptoms get harder to read

Sumatriptan can cause tightness or pressure in the chest, throat, or jaw. Usually this is harmless and passes quickly. But it can also, rarely, be a sign of a real heart problem, especially in someone with undiagnosed heart disease. When you've been drinking, your heart may already be racing and you may feel off in general, which makes it harder to tell a passing side effect from something serious. If chest symptoms are strong, last more than a few minutes, or come with shortness of breath, sweating, or pain spreading to your arm or jaw, treat it as an emergency.

### 4. Nausea and vomiting

Migraine often brings nausea, and alcohol irritates the stomach. If you vomit soon after swallowing a tablet, the dose may not be absorbed properly. That's part of why some people with nausea-heavy migraines are prescribed the nasal spray or injection instead.

## Can You Take Sumatriptan for a Hangover?

Usually, no. A hangover headache and a migraine are different things, and sumatriptan is designed for migraine.

A **hangover headache** tends to be a dull, pressing ache on both sides of the head, often with thirst, fatigue, a queasy stomach, and a general run-down feeling. It's driven by a mix of factors: dehydration, inflammation, poor sleep, and the by-products your body makes while breaking down alcohol. There's no good evidence that triptans help an ordinary hangover headache, and sumatriptan is only approved for migraine (and, for the injection, cluster headache).

A **migraine** is usually a throbbing pain, often on one side, that gets worse with movement and comes with sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, or sometimes an aura (visual changes such as zigzag lines or blind spots) beforehand.

The two can overlap. If you already have migraine, drinking can set off a true migraine attack the next morning, and in that case your usual triptan may be the right treatment. Doctors describe two patterns of alcohol-related headache in the International Classification of Headache Disorders: an **immediate** headache that starts within about three hours of drinking, and a **delayed** headache that shows up the next morning, which is essentially the hangover headache. People with migraine are more prone to both.

A rough way to tell them apart:

| Feature | Hangover headache | Migraine triggered by alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Where it hurts | Usually both sides, or all over | Often one side, sometimes switching |
| What it feels like | Dull, pressing ache | Throbbing, pulsing |
| Light and sound | Mildly annoying | Often hard to tolerate |
| Aura beforehand | No | Sometimes |
| Other symptoms | Thirst, fatigue, shakiness, general malaise | Nausea, worse with movement, need to lie in the dark |
| Do you have a migraine diagnosis? | Not required | Almost always yes |

If you don't have a migraine diagnosis, don't borrow someone else's sumatriptan for a hangover. It's a prescription drug for good reason: it isn't safe for people with certain heart and blood vessel conditions, and nobody has checked whether that's you. For ordinary hangover headaches, our guide to [hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers the options with better evidence.

## How Long Should You Wait to Drink After Taking Sumatriptan?

There's no official waiting period printed on the label, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours for everyone is guessing. What you can say with reasonable confidence:

- **Wait until the migraine has fully gone.** Drinking during an attack is the most likely way to make it worse or bring it back.
- **Give the drug a few hours.** With a half-life of about two hours, most of a tablet's effect has faded after several hours, and nearly all of it is cleared within about ten. Waiting at least until the drowsiness and dizziness are gone is sensible. Many people choose to skip drinking for the rest of the day after an attack.
- **Remember the second dose.** If the migraine comes back, the label allows a second tablet at least two hours after the first, up to a maximum of 200 mg in 24 hours for oral sumatriptan. If you've been drinking in that window, you add the side effects of a second dose on top of alcohol.
- **Hydrate and eat.** Dehydration and skipped meals are migraine triggers too.

### What about drinking first, then taking it?

If you've had a drink or two and a migraine starts, the general guidance is that taking your prescribed dose is reasonable, but stop drinking at that point. Don't take it on top of heavy drinking. If you've had a lot to drink, are vomiting, or feel very unwell, speak to a pharmacist or doctor, or call a nurse line, before taking anything.

## Rizatriptan (Maxalt), Imitrex, and Other Triptans

Many people searching for "sumatriptan and alcohol" are really on a different triptan. The good news is that the basic picture is the same for the whole class: no well-known direct chemical interaction with alcohol, but stacked drowsiness and dizziness, and the risk that alcohol triggers or prolongs the migraine.

**Imitrex** is simply the original brand name of sumatriptan. Everything in this guide about sumatriptan applies to Imitrex. The same goes for **Treximet**, a combination tablet of sumatriptan and naproxen, with one important addition covered below.

**Rizatriptan (Maxalt, Maxalt-MLT)** works in the same way and is also broken down mainly by MAO-A. It comes as a tablet and a melt-on-the-tongue wafer, usually 5 or 10 mg, with a typical maximum of 30 mg in 24 hours. Like sumatriptan, it can cause drowsiness, dizziness, and tiredness, which alcohol can make worse. One extra detail: if you take the blood pressure drug **propranolol**, your doctor will usually prescribe a lower rizatriptan dose, because propranolol raises rizatriptan levels in the blood. That's unrelated to alcohol, but worth knowing if you're on both.

**Other triptans** include zolmitriptan (Zomig), eletriptan (Relpax), naratriptan (Amerge), almotriptan, and frovatriptan (Frova). They differ in how fast they work and how long they last, and some, like eletriptan, are processed by liver enzymes that other drugs can affect. If you're on one of these, ask your pharmacist about your specific drug. The general advice in this guide still applies.

| Triptan | Brand names | Typical tablet sizes | Notes on alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sumatriptan | Imitrex, Imigran | 25, 50, 100 mg | No known direct interaction; side effects add up |
| Sumatriptan + naproxen | Treximet | Fixed combination | The naproxen part carries a stomach-bleeding warning with alcohol |
| Rizatriptan | Maxalt, Maxalt-MLT | 5, 10 mg | Same as sumatriptan; lower dose with propranolol |
| Zolmitriptan | Zomig | 2.5, 5 mg | Same general picture |
| Eletriptan | Relpax | 20, 40 mg | Same general picture; check other medicines |

Tablet sizes and maximums vary by country and product. Always follow the label and your prescriber's directions.

## Watch Out for Combination Products and Other Medicines

The bigger alcohol risks often come from what sumatriptan is paired with rather than sumatriptan itself.

### Naproxen and other NSAIDs

Treximet combines sumatriptan with naproxen, and many people take ibuprofen or naproxen alongside a triptan. These anti-inflammatory painkillers carry a label warning about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more alcoholic drinks a day, because alcohol and NSAIDs both irritate the stomach lining. If you use them together, take them with food and water and stick to the label dose. Our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the stomach and kidney risks in more detail.

### Excedrin Migraine and acetaminophen

Some people use Excedrin Migraine (acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine) or plain Tylenol on top of or instead of a triptan. Acetaminophen has a real interaction with alcohol in the liver, and aspirin adds stomach risk. See our guides to [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) before combining any of these with drinking.

### Antidepressants and serotonin syndrome

Sumatriptan acts on serotonin receptors, and the label carries a warning about **serotonin syndrome**, a rare but serious reaction from too much serotonin activity, when triptans are combined with SSRIs (such as sertraline or escitalopram) or SNRIs (such as venlafaxine or duloxetine). The FDA issued an alert about this in 2006. Later reviews by headache specialists, including a position paper from the American Headache Society, concluded that the real-world risk from combining triptans with these antidepressants appears to be low, and many people take both safely under a doctor's care. Still, the warning is on the label, and alcohol adds its own issues with antidepressants, such as extra drowsiness and worse mood. If you take an antidepressant, see our guides to [Zoloft and alcohol](/never-hungover/zoloft-and-alcohol) and [Lexapro and alcohol](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol), and ask your prescriber how all three fit together.

Signs of serotonin syndrome include agitation or confusion, a fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, sweating, fever, shivering, muscle twitching or stiffness, and diarrhea. If these appear after taking a triptan, get medical help right away.

### MAO inhibitors

Because sumatriptan and rizatriptan are broken down by MAO-A, they should not be taken with MAO inhibitor drugs (an older class of antidepressants) or within two weeks of stopping one. Some alcoholic drinks, especially tap beer and certain wines, also interact with MAO inhibitors. If you take an MAOI, your doctor needs to be in charge of both your migraine treatment and your drinking.

### Other migraine medicines

Don't take sumatriptan within 24 hours of another triptan or an ergotamine-type drug (such as dihydroergotamine). That's a label rule unrelated to alcohol, but it's easy to lose track of doses when you've been drinking.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You should talk to your doctor before mixing sumatriptan or any triptan with alcohol if you:

- **Have heart disease, a history of heart attack or stroke, or chest pain**, or have several risk factors such as smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes, or a strong family history. Triptans are not recommended for people with these conditions in the first place.
- **Have high blood pressure.** Triptans can raise blood pressure briefly, and heavy drinking raises it too.
- **Have liver disease.** Sumatriptan tablets are absorbed more fully in people with liver impairment, and the label advises lower doses or avoiding it in severe liver disease.
- **Take an antidepressant, an MAO inhibitor, or other serotonin-affecting drugs**, including some pain and cough medicines.
- **Use triptans or painkillers often.** Taking triptans on 10 or more days a month can lead to **medication overuse headache**, where the treatment itself starts causing more frequent headaches. If you're drinking and reaching for your triptan more and more, that's a conversation to have with your doctor.
- **Notice drinking is a reliable trigger.** If alcohol sets off your migraines regularly, a headache diary can help you and your doctor spot which drinks, amounts, and situations are the problem.

## When to See a Doctor

**Go to the emergency room or call 911 if, after taking sumatriptan (with or without alcohol), you have:**

- Chest pain, pressure, or tightness that is severe or doesn't fade within a few minutes
- Pain spreading to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, with sweating or shortness of breath
- Sudden weakness, numbness, or drooping on one side of your face or body, or trouble speaking
- A sudden, explosive headache that feels like the worst of your life
- Severe stomach pain, especially with bloody diarrhea
- Agitation, fever, fast heartbeat, and twitching or stiff muscles (possible serotonin syndrome)
- Hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing (possible allergic reaction)

**Book a regular appointment if:**

- Your migraines are getting more frequent or changing in character
- You're using a triptan or painkillers on more than about 8 to 10 days a month
- Alcohol keeps triggering attacks and you want a prevention plan
- Side effects like dizziness or chest tightness bother you, even if they pass

## Practical Tips If You Have Migraine and Want to Drink

Plenty of people with migraine still drink socially. A few habits make it less likely to end in an attack:

- **Know your triggers.** For some people it's red wine, for others dark spirits or any alcohol on an empty stomach. Our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) covers the usual suspects.
- **Keep the amount low.** Even people who tolerate alcohol often find there's a threshold. One drink may be fine where three aren't.
- **Drink water between drinks and eat first.** Dehydration and low blood sugar are migraine triggers on their own.
- **Protect your sleep.** A late night with broken sleep is a classic setup for a morning migraine.
- **Keep your treatment plan handy, and follow it.** Take your triptan early if an attack starts, then stop drinking.
- **Don't treat every morning-after headache as a migraine.** If it's a dull, all-over hangover ache, water, food, rest, and a simple painkiller used as directed are usually the better choice. Our guide to [headaches after one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) explains why some people react to even small amounts.

## Where Do Supplements Like DHM Fit?

People sometimes ask whether a hangover supplement could reduce alcohol-triggered headaches. Here's an honest view.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and intoxication. Most of the research is in animals and lab studies, with limited human data. There's no good evidence that DHM prevents migraines, and it has not been studied together with sumatriptan or other triptans. It does not change any of the safety advice in this guide.

If you're curious about trying it for ordinary hangovers on nights you do drink, check with your doctor or pharmacist first, especially if you take prescription medicines. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what's known. If you do want to try it, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when.

The most reliable step for migraine-prone drinkers remains the simple one: drink less, drink slower, and treat alcohol as a possible trigger.

## The Bottom Line

- Sumatriptan (Imitrex) has no known direct, dangerous chemical interaction with alcohol at normal doses.
- The real risks are stacked drowsiness and dizziness, alcohol triggering or prolonging the migraine, and harder-to-read side effects like chest tightness.
- Don't drink during an attack or soon after a dose. Wait until the migraine is gone and the drug's effects have worn off.
- A hangover headache isn't a migraine. Don't use sumatriptan for an ordinary hangover, and never take someone else's.
- Rizatriptan (Maxalt) and other triptans follow the same general rules. Combination products with naproxen or acetaminophen add their own alcohol warnings.
- If you take an antidepressant, have heart disease or high blood pressure, or use triptans often, talk to your doctor before drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking sumatriptan?**

There's no known direct, dangerous interaction between sumatriptan and alcohol at normal doses, and the label doesn't list alcohol as a contraindication. But it's best not to drink during a migraine attack or soon after a dose. Alcohol can make the migraine worse or bring it back, and both cause dizziness and drowsiness that add up. Ask your doctor if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, or take other medicines.

**How long after taking sumatriptan can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Sumatriptan's half-life is about two hours, so most of a dose has worn off after several hours and nearly all of it is cleared within about ten. A sensible approach is to wait until the migraine is completely gone and any drowsiness or dizziness has passed. Many people skip alcohol for the rest of the day after an attack.

**Can I take Imitrex with alcohol?**

Imitrex is the brand name of sumatriptan, so the same advice applies. There's no well-documented chemical interaction, but alcohol can trigger or prolong the migraine and adds to side effects like dizziness and drowsiness. Avoid drinking during an attack and talk to your doctor if you have heart problems or take antidepressants.

**Is it safe to mix rizatriptan (Maxalt) and alcohol?**

Rizatriptan follows the same general pattern as sumatriptan: no known direct dangerous interaction, but stacked drowsiness and dizziness and the risk that alcohol triggers or worsens the migraine. If you also take propranolol, your doctor will usually prescribe a lower rizatriptan dose, which is a separate issue from alcohol. Ask your pharmacist about your specific situation.

**Can sumatriptan cure a hangover headache?**

There's no good evidence that sumatriptan helps an ordinary hangover headache. It's designed and approved for migraine. If you have migraine and alcohol triggers a true migraine attack the next morning, your usual triptan may be appropriate. For a typical dull, all-over hangover ache, water, food, rest, and a simple painkiller used as directed are usually better choices.

**Does alcohol make sumatriptan less effective?**

There's no strong evidence that alcohol blocks sumatriptan chemically. In practice, though, alcohol can work against it by triggering or prolonging the migraine, causing dehydration, disrupting sleep, and making nausea worse. That can make an attack harder to control and more likely to return after the dose wears off.

**What are the dangerous signs after taking sumatriptan with alcohol?**

Get emergency help for chest pain or pressure that's severe or doesn't fade, pain spreading to your arm or jaw, sudden weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, a sudden explosive headache, or agitation with fever, fast heartbeat, and muscle twitching. These are rare, but they need care right away. Call 911 in an emergency.

**Can I take sumatriptan if I'm on an antidepressant and drink?**

The sumatriptan label warns about serotonin syndrome when triptans are combined with SSRIs or SNRIs. Headache specialists have concluded the real-world risk appears low, and many people take both under a doctor's care. Alcohol adds its own issues with antidepressants, such as extra drowsiness and low mood. Talk to your prescriber about how all three fit together.
